new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per word, located by the lexical class of the morphemes (the Interior Salish strong/weak system): a strong (inherently stressed) suffix takes the stress from any root; otherwise a strong root keeps stress on its root vowel; a weak root cedes stress to a vowel in the suffixal domain (a suffix vowel, or an epenthetic vowel when the weak suffixes are consonantal); an unsuffixed word is stressed on the root vowel. Prefixes are never stressed (Thomason & Thomason 2004). Unstressed vowels mostly reduce or delete, and Montana Salish/Kalispel speakers often truncate everything after the stressed vowel. Black argues the strong/weak classes reduce to underlying full vowel /i e u o a/ (strong) vs schwa-class /ə/ (weak), i.e. a vowel-quality-driven system rather than purely diacritic lexical marking.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed by Black 2006; Carlson 1972 (Spokane) notes secondary stress in longer utterances but leaves it unanalysed.
new_statements.exceptions: Some roots (e.g. the root 'take, grab, catch, sing') show inconsistent strong/weak stress behaviour across the dialect continuum (p. 38); apparent homophonous roots split into strong/weak minimal pairs under weak suffixation (Table 5); Thomason 1994 fn. 5 calls the Montana Salish stress system 'only partially predictable'; Post 1902 (apud Speck 1977: 24): 'Rules for the accent can hardly be given.. compound words retain the accent on the radical'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level primary stress in isolated (citation) word forms; the statement is made for 'the Spokane-Kalispel-Selis language' as a whole, with examples presented in Spokane-dialect spelling but restricted to roots whose strong/weak status is confirmed in two or more dialects (Spokane, Kalispel, Montana Seliš). Stressed syllables carry a high tone/F0 peak (Flemming et al. 2008).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Black 2006) describes 'the Spokane-Kalispel-Seliš language' as a single dialect continuum: Spokane (Glottolog spok1245, already catalogued from Carlson 1972) plus Kalispel (Lower Pend d'Oreille, Chewelah, Upper Pend d'Oreille) and Bitterroot Seliš/Montana Salish (= kali1308). Its example forms are printed in Spokane dialect, but the strong/weak stress generalisations are stated for the whole language and restricted to roots confirmed in two or more dialects, drawing on the author's Montana Seliš fieldnotes (1991-95), Vogt 1940 (Kalispel), Giorda 1877-79 and Pete 1998 (Flathead). Dialect-specific first-hand remarks for kali1308 varieties are weaker but consistent: Post 1902 apud Speck 1977: 24 (Kalispel/Pend d'Oreille, St. Ignatius: 'rules for the accent can hardly be given.. compound words retain the accent on the radical'), Thomason 1994 fn. 5 (Montana Salish stress 'only partially predictable'), Thomason & Thomason 2004 ('MSa has no stressed prefixes'). Vogt 1940, the Kalispel-proper grammar, was not reachable.

sources.locator: sec. 2.1 'Evidence for the strong/weak distinction', pp. 35-37 (PDF pp. 3-5)
sources.note: Sec. 2.1 (pp. 35-37) sets out the stress patterns of 'the Spokane-Kalispel-Selis language': unsuffixed forms stress a root vowel; with weak suffixes a strong root keeps primary stress while a weak root shifts it to a (epenthetic or suffixal) vowel in the suffixal domain; a strong suffix takes stress from any root. Argues the strong/weak distinction reduces to full vowel vs schwa underlyingly. Examples cited in Spokane dialect but limited to roots confirmed in two or more dialects; author's own Montana Seliš fieldnotes 1991-95 among sources.

sources.note: Sec. 2.8 'Stress' (p. 24) quotes Post (1902 MS, p. 2): 'Rules for the accent can hardly be given. Still, it may be taken as a general rule that compound words retain the accent on the radical. And since often the meaning of the word depends on the accent..'; Speck herself marks stress by deduction from Carlson's (1972) Spokan stress-assignment rules; fn. 10: a weak root is unstressed in combination with a suffix vowel.
